description: Hi! I'm Joe Tom, a first-time participant at the NASA Space Apps Challenge, competing solo as an engineering student. I'm excited to tackle the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by creating an interactive, engaging experience that helps prepare the next generation of space explorers. Looking forward to learning, building, and sharing my project with the community!!!
summary:
AstroPrep is a browser game that teaches students the trade-offs of running a lunar or Martian outpost. Players manage three core resources (power, oxygen, and radiation shielding) plus crew health over a 20-day mission, with only three crew hours per day. Every action has a real cost: expanding solar arrays uses up shielding material, making oxygen drains power, and building shielding costs power and crew effort. There is no free, safe choice.
Each day, a forecast warns of incoming space weather, based on real solar events from NASA's DONKI database, such as the 2003 Halloween storms and the 2017 X9.3 flare. Players must prepare shielding in advance, just as mission planners do. Events are randomized, so every playthrough differs, and when a mission fails the game explains why.
The event data is a curated static snapshot, clearly labeled in the app as not live, with NASA DONKI and NOAA cited as sources.
details:
What it does: AstroPrep is a browser game where students run a Moon or Mars outpost for 20 days. With only 3 crew hours a day, players balance power, oxygen, and radiation shielding. Every action has a cost, so there is no free "safe" choice. Random crew events and upgrades keep each run different, and when a mission fails, the game shows what hurt the crew most.
NASA data: On start, the game requests the last 30 days of solar flares from NASA's DONKI database. Moderate (M) and strong (X) flares become nightly events, and a 3-day forecast lets players raise shielding before a hit, as real mission planners do. If NASA can't be reached, it uses a saved snapshot of real past events (like the 2003 Halloween storms) and labels it SNAPSHOT. Static data is never shown as live.
Benefits and impact: It makes real engineering trade-offs fun for young learners without overwhelming them, using only three core resources. Players learn that power, oxygen, and shielding depend on each other, and that space weather is a real mission risk.
Tools: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with SVG graphics, NASA DONKI API, GitHub Pages for hosting. No installs needed, so it runs on any device with a browser.
Creativity: Science points buy upgrades, balance streaks raise the score, and the outpost reacts to your choices (shield glow, dimming lights, screen shake on big flares).
Factors considered: Clear data labelling, three resources to avoid overload, learning from failure without punishment, and honest labelling of simplifications. Hazard levels and damage numbers are game simplifications, not real radiation doses.

To play the game:https://joe-ui7878.github.io/NASA-Space-Apps-Challenge-2026/
